title: A letter to a king
hook: Nagarjuna's letter of advice to a royal friend

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that closed the gap: samsara and nirvana, no difference. Which ordinary thing did you give sacred attention to? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

The thinker who wrote of emptiness and two truths also had a friend who was a king. And to that friend, tradition says, he wrote a letter. Not a treatise for scholars. A letter, in verse, meant to be read by a busy man with a kingdom to run. It is known in Sanskrit as the Suhrllekha, the Letter to a Friend, and it survives in Tibetan and Chinese translations. The philosopher of emptiness, writing advice for a Tuesday. Today, the letter.
screen: `A PHILOSOPHER WITH A ROYAL FRIEND.` → `A LETTER, IN VERSE.` → `ADVICE FOR A BUSY KING.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. The letter begins humbly. Just as the wise honor an image of the Buddha even when it is carved from plain wood, it says, so please honor this advice, even if the verses are poor. The worth is in what it points to, not the polish. Second, the ordinary virtues. The letter does not start with emptiness. It speaks of generosity, of keeping ethical conduct, of patience, of not drinking to excess, of eating moderately, like taking medicine. These are things a king can actually do between meetings. Third, the eight worldly concerns. Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disgrace. The letter asks the king to meet all of them evenly, the good four and the hard four alike, since none of them lasts. For a ruler surrounded by flatterers and critics, that is practical advice. Fourth, the week behind us. The translators of the Pali Text Society, carrying old words into English. Sitting together, apart, on a screen. A last look back along the northern roads. Then Nagarjuna: the middle way, two truths, no difference. And now the same teacher, setting down plain advice in a friendly letter. The hardest ideas of the week still needed someone to write them kindly, for one person.
screen: `HONOR IT LIKE A WOODEN BUDDHA.` · `GENEROSITY, PATIENCE, MODERATION.` · `MEET THE EIGHT CONCERNS EVENLY.` · `A WEEK OF CARRYING THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `A LETTER OF ADVICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short letter of advice to yourself. In your head, or on paper if one is near. Start the way Nagarjuna did, gently: these are plain words, but take them seriously. Then write two or three lines. One about something you can actually do this week. One about meeting praise or blame a little more evenly. Write as a friend would, not a judge. Then sit with what you wrote, breathing quietly. The bell holds the time.
A letter to a king. Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend, verses of everyday advice for a ruler, offered like a Buddha carved from plain wood. Today's word.
screen: `A LETTER TO A KING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a letter of advice. Today, when praise or blame comes your way, try meeting it the same way, as one of the eight that come and go. That's the week. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend is studied in Tibetan Buddhism as practical advice for lay life, and teachers often explain the eight worldly concerns from it to lay students.

fork.reveal: tradition says Nagarjuna wrote his royal friend a letter: generosity, patience, moderation, and meeting the eight worldly concerns evenly.

original.note: Sanskrit Suhrllekha: suhrd, a friend, and lekha, a letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a philosopher of emptiness writes only for philosophers.
what it means: tradition says Nagarjuna wrote a friendly letter of everyday advice to a king, asking him to honor it like a plain wooden Buddha.
what a scholar hears: the Suhrllekha, preserved in Tibetan and Chinese, teaches generosity, ethics, moderation and the eight worldly concerns.

notes: The Suhrllekha is paraphrased throughout; no public-domain English translation is on the validator list (Wenzel's 1886 translation from Tibetan exists but is not listed).
Opening image (honor an image of the Sugata even if made of wood, so honor this poor verse): confirm placement in the opening verses.
Eating 'like taking medicine' and 'not drinking to excess': confirm these appear in the letter as paraphrased.
Eight worldly concerns (gain/loss, pleasure/pain, praise/blame, fame/disgrace) to be met evenly: the count is the letter's own list; confirm.
The royal friend is traditionally identified as a Satavahana king; no name or date given under the claims rule.
Survival 'in Tibetan and Chinese translations' with the Sanskrit original lost: confirm.
The index title 'A letter to a king' could also suggest the Ratnavali (Precious Garland), also addressed to a king; this script follows the outline's 'royal friend' and uses the Suhrllekha.
